passage:
Last Tuesday, in the middle of the winter prelims, I did something I'm still a bit ashamed of. I had spent six hours on physics numericals at the dining table while fog pressed against the window. By eight my brain felt like wet paper.
Payal, my little sister, asked, "Ganga Didi, roti or the khichdi Mumma left?" I couldn't decide, so I tore open a family packet of chips and ate it standing at the fridge.
Then my friend Tanvi sent three photos of dresses for her cousin's wedding. "Which one?? Help!!" I typed "whatever u like" and turned the phone face down.
In the morning, after sleep and a proper breakfast, I saw her reply: "ok 🙁". It wasn't that I didn't care. I had simply run out of choosing.

qa.q: What did Ganga eat instead of choosing between roti and khichdi?
qa.a: She tore open a family packet of chips and ate it standing at the fridge.

qa.q: Why did the chips and the quick reply feel like the only choices Ganga could make that evening?
qa.a: After six hours of numericals Ganga felt drained, with a brain "like wet paper", so anything that needed a decision felt too heavy and the easiest option won.

qa.q: What could Ganga try on the next long study day?
qa.a: She could settle dinner and reply to friends during an afternoon break, or tell friends she'll answer properly after sleep.

qa.q: How might Tanvi have felt reading "whatever u like"?
qa.a: Tanvi may have felt brushed off and a little hurt, since she was excited about the dresses and wanted Ganga's help 🙁

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after hours of study, grabs junk food and sends a quick reply because choosing has worn her out.

passage:
Subject: Help, Didi

Hi Shalini Didi,
Diwali week in the hostel is chaos, and I think it's frying my brain. Today I decided which mess slot to take, whether to drop the stats elective, which group to join for the project, whether to come home on Friday or Saturday, what to tell Mummy about the hostel form, and which three internships to shortlist.
By nine I was done. When Rahul asked about our group presentation, I said, "Let's decide tomorrow." Then I ordered a huge box of fried chicken I didn't even want and watched episodes till two. I still haven't opened the internship forms, and they close on Friday.
This keeps happening. In the mornings I'm sensible. At night I'm a different person.
How did you manage in your final year?
Your useless little brother,
Nitin

qa.q: When do the internship forms close?
qa.a: They close on Friday.

qa.q: Why does Nitin order food he didn't want and watch episodes till two?
qa.a: After deciding so many things all day, Nitin felt worn out and overwhelmed, so ordering and watching felt easier than any real choice, and avoiding the forms brought a moment of relief.

qa.q: What would you advise Nitin?
qa.a: Nitin could open the internship forms in the morning, the sensible time of day, and turn small choices like the mess slot into fixed routines so fewer decisions pile up by night.

qa.q: How might Rahul feel when Nitin says "Let's decide tomorrow"?
qa.a: Rahul may feel stalled and a bit frustrated, since the group presentation still has no plan.

grounding: Shows a student who, after a day full of small decisions, slides into impulse and avoidance in the evening.

passage:
Noa's mornings in Copenhagen looked almost boring from outside: the same oat porridge, the same three grey jumpers hung by weekday, the same cycle route to the studio. Her flatmate teased her about it. Noa just shrugged. "Fewer things to decide before nine."
By nine she was at her desk with the hardest task of the day already open.
At quarter to six Hana, her project partner, rushed over, coat half on. "The builders called again about the kindergarten playground. Can we just pick one now? I'm starving."
Noa looked at the clock, then at Hana's pale face. "Neither of us should pick anything right now. Tomorrow at nine, both files open, coffee in hand."
Hana groaned, then laughed. The next morning they chose in twenty minutes.

qa.q: What does Noa eat every morning?
qa.a: The same oat porridge.

qa.q: Why does Noa refuse to choose a builder at quarter to six?
qa.a: She is wary of deciding when they are both hungry and rushed, and feels calm and sure that a fresh morning will give a better choice.

qa.q: Which of Noa's habits could a busy young professional copy?
qa.a: They could turn small things like breakfast and clothes into routines and keep big choices for the morning, when they are fed and fresh.

qa.q: What is it like for Hana when Noa says not now?
qa.a: Hana feels frustrated at first and groans because she wants it over with, but she ends up relieved when they choose in twenty minutes the next morning.

grounding: Shows a professional using routines for small choices and saving an important decision for a fresh, fed morning.

passage:
On the evening before Eid, the toy shop in the bazaar was packed, and the shopkeeper was already pulling down one shutter. "Ten minutes!" he called.
Afreen stood before a wall of dolls, cars, whistles and puzzles, clutching her Eidi. Her lip began to wobble. She picked up a car, put it back, touched a doll, and burst into tears.
Rekha Aunty crouched beside her and held up just three things. "Kite, tea set or ball?"
Afreen stopped crying, looked at each one, and hugged the tea set. She smiled all the way home.

qa.q: How many things did Rekha Aunty hold up?
qa.a: She held up just three things: a kite, a tea set and a ball.

qa.q: Why did Afreen burst into tears in front of the wall of toys?
qa.a: There were so many toys and so little time that she felt overwhelmed and could not settle on one.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Rekha Aunty holding up only three things worked, because Afreen could look at each one and choose calmly.

qa.q: What would change if Rekha Aunty had said, "Pick anything you like"?
qa.a: Afreen would probably keep crying or grab the nearest toy, and she might not feel as happy with it on the way home.

grounding: Shows a young child freezing and crying in front of too many toys, and choosing happily from a small selection.

passage:
The Shimla ice-cream parlour was crowded on Christmas Eve, and snow-wet coats steamed in the queue. The board above the counter listed thirty-two flavours.
"Your turn, Nihal," said Urmila Mausi.
Nihal read the board from top to bottom. Butterscotch? Rose? Blueberry swirl? Behind him someone sighed loudly. The server tapped the scoop on the glass.
"Mango," he blurted.
At the table his cousin Tara was licking a scoop of chocolate chip. Nihal stared at it, then at his mango. "I should have got that." Halfway through he added, "Or rose. Rose might have been the best."
Urmila Mausi laughed. "Last summer the stall had four flavours, and you finished yours in two minutes and never looked back."

qa.q: How many flavours did the board list?
qa.a: The board listed thirty-two flavours.

qa.q: Why does Nihal keep wishing he had picked something else?
qa.a: With so many flavours, every one he didn't pick still seems possibly better, so he feels unsure and disappointed with his mango even while eating it.

qa.q: What could Urmila Mausi try with Nihal next time?
qa.a: She could help him narrow the board to three flavours he likes before he reaches the counter, so the pick is quick and feels settled.

qa.q: How might the person sighing behind Nihal see his long wait?
qa.a: They were probably impatient, standing in a crowded, steamy queue while he read all thirty-two flavours.

grounding: Shows a child taking ages over a long menu and then wishing he had picked a different flavour.

passage:
By the end of the January sales in Manchester, Sami's spreadsheet held twenty-three phones, with columns for battery, camera, weight and reviews. He had watched so many comparison videos that the phones blurred into one glossy rectangle.
"Just pick," Amara said, scrolling on the one she had bought in ten minutes at the corner shop. "Mine's great."
On the last day of the sale, after the top two sold out, he finally clicked "buy" on the one ranked third.
It arrived on Thursday. It was fast and the photos were sharp. But that night Sami opened the spreadsheet again and stared at numbers one and two. "Maybe the second one's battery..." he muttered.
Amara, eating toast across the table, shook her head. "You've got a good phone and you're still sulking about two you don't own."

qa.q: How many phones were in Sami's spreadsheet?
qa.a: Twenty-three phones.

qa.q: Why is Sami still unsatisfied with a phone that works well?
qa.a: Having compared so many, he feels unsure and a bit regretful, since each phone he didn't buy still seems like it might have been better.

qa.q: What could Sami try the next time he has to choose?
qa.a: He could decide the three features that matter most, cut the list to a shortlist of three, and stop comparing once he has bought.

qa.q: How does Amara see Sami's spreadsheet habit?
qa.a: She finds it puzzling, because she chose hers in ten minutes and is happy with it, while he sulks about phones he doesn't own.

grounding: Shows a student comparing dozens of phones and feeling less satisfied with the final pick than a simpler choice would allow.

passage:
Sunday, 14 July
Flat hunting, day three. The old me would have spent six weeks on this and still cried at the end. Today I tried the method properly.
Before opening a single listing, I wrote three must-haves on a sticky note: under forty minutes to the office, a window that opens onto something green, a landlord who replies within a day. Everything else is a nice-to-have.
Jatin kept sending links. "Jahnavi, this one has a rooftop pool!" Not on the sticky note. Deleted.
By noon I had a shortlist of three. Saw all of them by five. The Indiranagar one isn't perfect: small kitchen, noisy road. But it ticks all three.
I paid the token and felt calm. Jatin thinks I rushed. Maybe. But tonight I'm sleeping, not scrolling.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Three must-haves: under forty minutes to the office, a window that opens onto something green, and a landlord who replies within a day.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel after paying the token, and why?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt calm, because the flat ticked all three must-haves, so the small kitchen and noisy road did not reopen the search.

qa.q: What small step made the search manageable?
qa.a: Writing the must-haves before opening any listing, which let Jahnavi delete links like the rooftop pool and reach a shortlist of three by noon.

qa.q: Why might Jatin react differently to the choice?
qa.a: Jatin thinks it was rushed, perhaps because extras like a rooftop pool seemed worth more searching.

grounding: Shows a person setting criteria first, keeping a shortlist of three and choosing a good-enough flat rather than a perfect one.

passage:
Paper stars hung in the corridor of Aadhya's Chandigarh school for Christmas week when the notice for the inter-school poetry slam went up. Entries closed Friday.
"You have to," Jasleen said, tapping the poster. "Your monsoon poem made Ma'am cry."
Aadhya pictured it: the auditorium, her voice cracking on the second verse, the judges' blank faces, kids from other schools whispering. Worse, she pictured the ride home knowing she'd been bad. "If I don't enter, at least I can't lose," she said.
On Thursday Jasleen slid a form onto her desk, already half filled. Aadhya held the pen over it for a long moment, then tucked it into her notebook.
On Saturday Jasleen texted the list of finalists. Aadhya read every name and felt a small, sour ache she hadn't expected.

qa.q: When did entries for the poetry slam close?
qa.a: Entries closed Friday.

qa.q: Why does not entering feel safer to Aadhya?
qa.a: She is afraid of failing on stage and of the ride home knowing she'd been bad, so not trying feels like a way to avoid that regret.

qa.q: What could Aadhya try the next time a chance like this comes?
qa.a: She could picture both regrets side by side, a shaky voice on stage and reading the finalists' list from home, and ask herself which she would rather live with.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel when the form stays in Aadhya's notebook?
qa.a: Jasleen may feel disappointed, since she believed in the monsoon poem enough to half fill the form herself.

grounding: Shows a teenager who skips a competition because the regret of failing feels worse than the regret of never trying.

passage:
"Happy New Year in two hours," Hrithik said, handing over a paper cup of tea on the hostel terrace. "So? Studio or the bank?"
"Bank. I signed today."
"Lokesh! You spent all year talking about the animation studio. They called you back twice."
"And if the studio shuts in a year? Everyone at home would say, see, he threw away a proper job."
"And if you sit in the bank for five years drawing on sticky notes?"
"Then at least nobody can say I made a mistake."
"Somebody can. You'll be the one saying it."
Lokesh laughed, but it came out thin. Below them the first fireworks went up early. He watched them without looking at Hrithik. "Let's just enjoy tonight, yaar."

qa.q: How many times did the studio call Lokesh back?
qa.a: They called him back twice.

qa.q: What is Lokesh most afraid of if he chooses the studio?
qa.a: He is afraid the studio might shut and everyone at home would say he threw away a proper job, so the bank feels safe from blame even though he wanted animation.

qa.q: What could help Lokesh weigh the choice more fairly?
qa.a: He could write down what he might regret in five years on each path, including drawing on sticky notes at the bank, and talk it over with someone he trusts.

qa.q: How does Hrithik see the decision?
qa.a: Hrithik is worried that Lokesh is choosing to avoid other people's blame and will end up blaming himself instead.

grounding: Shows a young adult choosing the safe job so no one can call it a mistake, while the regret of not trying already shows.

passage:
Mentoring notes, Diwali week
Kishore came to see me again today, his third visit since September. He has had three paths in front of him: the team lead role here, a master's offer in Pune, and a friend's start-up. He has not said no to any of them.
He told me, "If I pick one and it goes wrong, I'll always wonder about the other two." His eyes kept drifting to the paper lanterns in the office window as he spoke.
Meanwhile the master's deadline passed last week, and the start-up has found someone else. The team lead post, the only door left, closes when we return after Diwali.
I didn't tell him which to choose. I asked him to write down what waiting has already cost him, and to come back on Monday with a yes or a no.
Varun, senior mentor

qa.q: What happened to the master's offer?
qa.a: The master's deadline passed last week.

qa.q: Why does Kishore keep all three paths open?
qa.a: He is afraid that if he picks one and it goes wrong he'll always wonder about the other two, so committing feels riskier than waiting.

qa.q: What did Varun ask Kishore to do, and how might it help?
qa.a: Varun asked Kishore to write down what waiting has already cost him and to return on Monday with a yes or a no, which makes the hidden cost of delay visible.

qa.q: How might the friend with the start-up see Kishore's delay?
qa.a: The friend may have felt let down or tired of waiting, and moved on by finding someone else.

grounding: Shows a young professional who delays committing for fear of regretting the road not taken, until the delay itself closes doors.
